newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-Regrets haunt China returnees but life improves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Regrets haunt China returnees but life improves.

text.p: They came back to their Chinese motherland full of hope and idealism and carved out fertile fields from the malarial wastes of its southernmost island.

But for many of the thousands of returnees who built the Xinglong Overseas Chinese Farm in tropical Hainan province, the decision to come back to the political maelstrom that has been 20th century China was a source of decades of bitter regret.

While hard work and mercantile skill enriched ethnic Chinese compatriots across southeast Asia, those who journeyed back to their ancestral homeland laboured for decades in poverty only recently eased by China's economic reforms.

"In Indonesia our whole family could live on the money my father made. My mother, six brothers and I didn't have to work at all. Of course I wish I had stayed," said one returnee who toiled for years tapping the farm's state-owned rubber trees.
Patriotism and communist ardour brought waves of emigrant families back from Indonesia, Malaysia and other overseas Chinese communities in the years after China's 1949 revolution.
Thousands more were forced to return in later decades by anti-Chinese sentiment in the lands where they had settled.

Beijing's communist mandarins sent the returnees -- many of whom were born abroad -- to Hainan, a disease-ridden and lightly-populated frontier zone that for centuries had been used as a place of exile for disgraced imperial officials.
"Life was very hard, but we turned the wasteland into rubber trees and coffee plants," said Guo Jinglian, 56, who now owns a shop in dusty Xinglong town at the heart of the sprawling farm.
The returnees tamed the wilderness and fought off disease, but found it impossible to avoid the political turmoil that has tormented China throughout a turbulent century.
POLITICALLY SUSPECT, IDEOLOGICALLY DIVIDED

In 1966, former Chairman Mao Zedong plunged the nation into 10 years of ultra-leftist chaos by launching the Cultural Revolution, when youthful Red Guards waged war on anything seen as smacking of tradition or foreign imperialism.

The overseas Chinese, suspect because of their time abroad, suffered discrimination from stay-at-home radicals -- and were themselves deeply divided into rival ideological camps, Xinglong residents say.
"There was fighting among the overseas Chinese. I too carried a gun," said shopkeeper Guo, who was born in Indonesia and came to China in 1960.
"The army came with artillery... many people died," he said.
Turmoil along with communist bans on free enterprise kept the farmers poor and oppressed, said another returnee, who spent two years in a labour camp for trying to flee to Hong Kong.

"In Indonesia there was freedom: if you had the money you could move about as you pleased -- but in China there is no freedom and you aren't even allowed to say there is no freedom," said the villager, who declined to be identified.
"I wish I had never come back," he said.
While regrets still linger, Xinglong's returnees have seized on free-market economic reforms launched by Mao's successor Deng Xiaoping as a chance to turn their past into profit.

The farm remains state-owned but has been reorganised into a company whose 10,000 "workers" have control of their own fields and where sideline jobs are now the main source of income for many of the 25,000 residents.
HOT BATHS MAKE LIFE EASIER

Motorcycles are proliferating and tourism is transforming what must be one of China's most cosmopolitan rural areas, where many residents can still chatter in Malay or Vietnamese and some can even trot out rusty English or Dutch.

Restaurants serve half-remembered curries and satays and the town is dotted with cafes -- a rarity in tea-sipping China -- where bitter coffee is served Southeast Asian style with heaped sugar and condensed milk.
But the greatest attraction for Xinglong visitors wells up from deep underground.
"We have very good hot springs," said farm vice director Liang Senkui, adding that tourist numbers had swelled following the creation of the Xinglong Overseas Chinese Tourist Village.

The change has been dramatic. A quiet park where just six years ago one sleepy hostel offered occasional visitors a no-frills hot spring experience has been buried by a bustling tourist town of more than 30 hotels and scores of restaurants.
Guests bathe in hot spring swimming pools with a view of distant mountains and the tropical sky, while outside pimps on motorcycles cruise the new-built roads for custom.
Accommodation ranges from plush marbled hotels to an Islamic-style state-owned guesthouse festooned with propaganda posters of Saddam Hussein.

"Things are getting better -- more and more people are coming, especially Indonesians, Singaporeans, Japanese and Taiwanese," said Wang Tingquan, 62, who performs old Southeast Asian songs for tips at a Tourist Village restaurant.
"I paid for my house with the songs I sing," said Wang, a gold-toothed crooner who returned to China to study in 1957.
The new affluence among some Xinglong residents had helped ease the pain of comparison with the luxurious lifestyles of overseas Chinese communities elsewhere, said shopkeeper Guo.
"It all depends on how well you are doing," he said. "Now I have money and business is good, but the people who still have to labour definitely feel regret."
